claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §11.1 Object-oriented programming basics; §11.2 Classes and instances

artifact.q: A program uses the same class to make two playlist objects. What is the best expectation about their data and behavior?
op: Each playlist has its own attributes, while the class methods are shared.
Both playlists must share one combined set of attributes.
The class keeps the attributes, and each object gets a different method set.
Methods belong only to the first playlist created.
artifact.ex: Correct: each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, and the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance. A common misconception is that one object's data is automatically shared by all others, or that methods are duplicated separately for each object.

artifact.q: When an individual entity is generated from a class definition, what is it termed?
artifact.ex: Option C is correct because individual objects created from a class are called instances. Option A is incorrect because the class is the blueprint. Option B is incorrect because a method is a behavior defined by the class.

claims: A variable is a name that refers to a stored value; the assignment operator = binds the name on the left to the value produced on the right (for objects it binds the reference, so no copy is made).
A statement sets a variable to a value using the assignment operator (=), with the name on the left and the value on the right.
Assignment is not mathematical equality — = copies a value into a variable rather than asserting two sides are equal.
A variable name may contain letters, digits, and underscores and be any length, but cannot start with a digit.
Variable names are case-sensitive, so total and Total are two different variables.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §1.3 Variables

artifact.q: Which characteristic describes the naming convention for a variable in Python?
op: A: Variable names must start with a letter, but can contain digits.
B: Variable names are case-sensitive, meaning 'Total' and 'total' are distinct.
C: Variable names cannot contain underscores.
D: Variable names must be the same length as the value they store.
artifact.ex: Option B is correct because variable names are case-sensitive, so 'Total' and 'total' are two different variables. Option A is a misconception because variable names cannot start with a digit, and Option C is incorrect because names can contain underscores.

artifact.q: Which variable name is valid in Python?
artifact.ex: B is correct because variable names may include letters, digits, and underscores, and they cannot start with a digit. A is the common mistake: it starts with a digit. The other choices use an invalid hyphen or a space.

claims: Silicate minerals, built from the silicon-oxygen tetrahedron, are the most abundant rock-forming minerals; the way tetrahedra link together defines the major silicate structures.
The silicon-oxygen tetrahedron (SiO4) is one silicon atom at the center bonded to four oxygen atoms at the corners.
Tetrahedra link by sharing corner oxygen atoms into chains, sheets, or three-dimensional frameworks.
How much oxygen is shared between tetrahedra controls the silicate group — isolated tetrahedra, single chains, sheets, or frameworks like quartz.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §3.1 Silicate minerals

artifact.df: Tetrahedra link by sharing corner oxygen atoms into chains, sheets, or three-dimensional frameworks.
artifact.mi: Tetrahedral linkage is the process where silicon-oxygen tetrahedra connect.
artifact.cx: Tetrahedral linkage is the process of linking silicon-oxygen tetrahedra by sharing corner oxygen atoms.

artifact.df: A basic silicate unit with one silicon atom in the center and four oxygen atoms at the corners.
artifact.eg: A single SiO4 unit in a silicate mineral structure.
artifact.mi: It is a flat ring of atoms.
artifact.cx: The atom arrangement is three-dimensional, with one central silicon bonded to four oxygens.

claims: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core; the upper mantle's asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.
The mantle sits below the crust and above the core.
The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel.
The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.1 Earth's interior

artifact.df: The planet’s central metallic region, made mostly of iron and nickel and divided into liquid and solid layers.
artifact.eg: Seismic evidence shows distinct liquid and solid parts within the deep center of Earth.
artifact.mi: It is a single uniform solid sphere.
artifact.cx: It has both liquid and solid layers, and it is mostly iron and nickel.

artifact.df: The primary elements found in the planet's innermost region.
artifact.eg: The presence of iron and nickel in the core.
artifact.mi: Assuming the core is composed of the same material as the outer crust.
artifact.cx: The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel (Claim 2).

claims: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core; the upper mantle's asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.
The mantle sits below the crust and above the core.
The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel.
The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.1 Earth's interior

artifact.q: A lab group notes a rock layer that lies below the crust and above the core. Which Earth layer is this?
artifact.ex: The mantle fits because it is the layer below the crust and above the core. A common misconception is to choose the core because it is deeper, but the core is below the mantle, not between crust and core.

artifact.q: Which layer of Earth is described as solid rock that flows slowly due to convection?
artifact.ex: The asthenosphere is the correct choice because it is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat (Claim 3). The most plausible misconception is selecting the rocky mantle, which is described as thick and solid rock, not flowing.

claims: In music theory, an interval is a difference in pitch between two sounds.
In physical terms, an interval is the ratio between two sonic frequencies.
Intervals between successive notes of a scale are also known as scale steps.

artifact.q: What is the definition of an interval in music theory?
op: A. The ratio between two sonic frequencies.
B. A difference in pitch between two sounds.
C. The ratio between two notes in a scale.
D. The difference in pitch between two sounds.
artifact.ex: Option B is correct because an interval is defined as a difference in pitch between two sounds (Claim 0). Option A is incorrect because the ratio between two sonic frequencies is a physical term, not the primary music theory definition.

artifact.q: In an analysis note, a student says the distance between two pitches is being described. Which term fits best?
artifact.ex: Pitch difference is correct because an interval is defined as the difference in pitch between two sounds. A common misconception is to treat the same idea as a frequency ratio; that ratio is the physical description, not the basic theoretical one.

claims: In music, form refers to the structure of a musical composition or performance.
The term "binary form" is used to describe a musical piece with two sections that are about equal in length.
Musical form unfolds over time through the expansion and development of these ideas.
Form in music is the result of the interaction of the four structural elements described above [sound, harmony, melody, rhythm].
Subdivisions of each large musical unit are shown by lowercase letters (a, b, and so on).
The next level concerns the entire structure of any single self-contained musical piece or movement.

artifact.df: The result of the interaction of sound, harmony, melody, and rhythm.
artifact.eg: Examining how sound, harmony, melody, and rhythm interact to create the piece.
artifact.mi: A single musical element like rhythm.
artifact.cx: The interaction of the four structural elements described above [sound, harmony, melody, rhythm].

artifact.df: A two-part design with sections of about equal length.
artifact.eg: A short piece divided into two roughly equal sections fits this description.
artifact.mi: It means any piece with two themes.
artifact.cx: The key feature is two sections that are about equal in length.

claims: Accessibility and usability evaluation combines standards-based conformance checks with observation of representative users completing realistic tasks.
WCAG organizes web accessibility around the principles perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust.
Evaluation with disabled and older users can find barriers that conformance evaluation alone does not reveal.
A usability test observes users attempting to use a product or service while thinking aloud.
A single disabled participant's experience should not be generalized to all people with disabilities.
sourceContext.license: W3C Document License and U.S. Government Work

artifact.df: A web-accessibility framework organized around four principles.
artifact.eg: A course team checks whether a prototype is perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust before user testing.
artifact.mi: It is mainly a checklist for visual design polish.
artifact.cx: The principles guide accessibility review beyond appearance and support structured conformance checks.

artifact.df: A method of observing users attempting to use a product or service while thinking aloud.
artifact.eg: Watching a user struggle to find the 'submit' button on a prototype while verbalizing their confusion.
artifact.mi: Usability testing is just watching users without any verbal feedback.
artifact.cx: Usability testing is observing users attempting to use a product or service while thinking aloud (Claim 3).

claims: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.
Personas are one way to present research findings so other people can understand and share them.
User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.
Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs.
Keeping each user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is being met.

artifact.df: A shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs.
artifact.eg: A persona detailing the needs of 'Busy Professionals' for a new scheduling app.
artifact.mi: This is just a list of user requests.
artifact.cx: This is a research-based persona, which links design choices to evidence.

artifact.df: A shareable profile built from research to represent a user group with similar behavior and needs.
artifact.eg: After interviews and observation, a studio team creates a persona for commuter students who need quick mobile checkout.
artifact.mi: It is just a fictional character invented to sound realistic.
artifact.cx: A persona should be grounded in evidence so design choices stay connected to what research shows about the group.

claims: A task flow analysis diagrams the steps and decision points through which a user interacts with a system to reach a defined goal.
Task flow analysis can validate the team's understanding of user goals, common scenarios, and tasks.
A task flow should show how a user progresses through tasks to accomplish a goal.
Task flow analysis should surface obstacles that stand between users and their goals.
The diagram may include multiple possible paths, task sequences, and decision points.

artifact.df: The process of confirming the team's grasp of user objectives, common scenarios, and required tasks.
artifact.eg: Reviewing a flow to ensure it accurately reflects how users typically complete a specific task.
artifact.mi: Assuming the analysis automatically proves the team understands the user's ultimate goal.
artifact.cx: Task flow analysis can validate the team's understanding of user goals, common scenarios, and tasks.

artifact.df: A moment in the flow where the user's next path depends on a choice or condition.
artifact.eg: After entering a password, the flow branches to success, error, or reset steps.
artifact.mi: It is the same as any screen in the process.
artifact.cx: A decision point creates branching paths; a screen may contain one, but not every screen is a decision point.
